involves_russia.hypothesis: This text mentions Russia, the Soviet Union, the Russian Empire or Russian people.
involves_russia.note: Backstop for keyword hits. Below the threshold the paragraph passes untouched (the keyword was incidental). Wording chosen 2026-11-20 against the seed drafts: recall 0.86 / precision 0.68 at 0.5. The guide's wording 'This text is about Russia, the Russian state or Russian people.' had recall 0.53 (missed Tsarist / Soviet history).

text: Forecasters expect a sharp drop in temperatures across eastern Poland from Thursday as a mass of cold, dry air moves in from western Russia. Night frosts of minus eight degrees are possible in Białystok and Lublin, and drivers are advised to fit winter tyres before the weekend. The cold spell should ease by Monday when milder Atlantic air returns from the west.
note: Russia is named as a real place (source of an air mass); nothing else about Russia is discussed.

text: Our chess club had a lovely evening last Friday. Our guest speaker, a retired bridge engineer who grew up in Russia and moved to Ireland thirty years ago, told us how he learned the game from his grandfather on a board with two missing pawns, replaced by buttons. He then played a simultaneous exhibition against twelve members and lost only one game, to our youngest junior.
note: Refers to a person who grew up in Russia; the topic is a local chess club, not Russian culture.

text: A Russian-flagged cargo vessel ran aground early on Sunday in a narrow fjord north of Tromsø, Norwegian coastal authorities said. The ship, carrying frozen fish, was refloated at high tide with the help of two tugboats. No injuries or leaks were reported, and the crew of fourteen remained on board while divers inspected the hull for damage.
note: A Russian ship is mentioned; the story is a local maritime incident, not business, politics or war.

text: Visitors to the city zoo can now see the two Amur tigers that arrived last month from a breeding centre in Russia. The young male and female spent several weeks in quarantine and are now exploring their new enclosure, which includes a pool and a heated rock. Keepers say the pair are curious and enjoy chasing pumpkins filled with meat.
note: Russia is named as the animals' origin; the paragraph is about a zoo.

text: The Finnish consulate reminds applicants that appointments must be booked online. Russian citizens applying for a residence permit on the basis of family ties should bring a valid passport, two photos, a marriage or birth certificate with a certified translation, and proof of accommodation. Incomplete applications will not be accepted, and processing can take up to four months.
note: Refers to Russian citizens as a group of applicants; administrative information, no politics or culture.

text: My great-uncle Tomas was a sailor all his life. In 1962 his ship docked in a port in the Soviet Union for three days, and he always told us about the enormous cranes and the sailors who traded cigarettes for his chewing gum. He kept a small postcard of the harbour on his kitchen wall until he died, next to postcards from Lisbon and Montreal.
note: Explicitly names the Soviet Union; a family anecdote rather than a discussion of Soviet history.

text: For a quick Russian dressing, whisk together half a cup of mayonnaise, two tablespoons of ketchup, a teaspoon of horseradish, a splash of Worcestershire sauce and a pinch of paprika. Stir in finely chopped pickles if you like some crunch. It keeps for five days in the fridge and is the classic sauce for a Reuben sandwich.
note: 'Russian dressing' is an American condiment name; Russia itself is not referred to.

text: Putting your entire retirement savings into a single meme stock is basically playing Russian roulette with your future. Diversify across index funds, keep an emergency fund of at least six months of expenses, and only gamble with money you can truly afford to lose. Boring investing is usually the kind that actually works over thirty years.
note: 'Russian roulette' is an idiom for reckless risk; no reference to Russia.

text: The city council of Moscow, Idaho, voted on Tuesday to extend the downtown farmers market until the end of October. Vendors had asked for the extra weeks because of the late apple harvest on the Palouse. The market will run every Saturday morning on Main Street, and the University of Idaho student band will play at the closing event.
note: Moscow, Idaho is a US town; nothing refers to Russia.

text: St. Petersburg, Florida, is known for its long waterfront park system, the Dalí Museum and an average of 361 days of sunshine a year. The Pier District has restaurants, a splash pad and boat tours of Tampa Bay. Visitors can easily reach the Gulf beaches by trolley, and the downtown art scene includes dozens of outdoor murals.
note: St. Petersburg, Florida is a US city; no reference to Russia.

text: To change the display language, open Settings, select 'Region & Language' and choose from the drop-down menu: English, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Russian, Japanese or Chinese. The app will restart automatically. Your saved projects and keyboard shortcuts are not affected by the change, and you can switch back at any time.
note: 'Russian' appears only as an item in a software language list.

text: I've been using the SteelSeries 'Siberia' headset for gaming for about a year. The ear cups are comfortable for long sessions, the microphone is clear on Discord, and the cable is long enough for a desk setup. My only complaint is that the headband padding started to flake after ten months. For the price, still a solid recommendation.
note: 'Siberia' is a product name of a headset; no reference to Russia or the region.

text: The novel is built like a Russian doll: a story inside a diary inside a letter inside a court record. Every time you open one layer, another narrator appears and quietly contradicts the last one. It is exhausting at times, but the final chapter, where the outermost frame cracks open, makes the whole structure feel worth it.
note: 'Russian doll' is a metaphor for a nested structure; the novel and its subject are not Russian.

text: Today's core workout: three rounds of twenty Russian twists, fifteen leg raises, a forty-five-second plank and ten slow mountain climbers per side. Keep your back straight during the twists and rotate from the ribs, not the arms. If you want more challenge, hold a light dumbbell or a water bottle. Rest one minute between rounds.
note: 'Russian twist' is the name of an exercise; Russia is not referred to.

text: The Russian animated series 'Masha and the Bear' has become one of the most-watched cartoons in the world. Each short episode follows a mischievous little girl who causes chaos in the forest home of a patient retired circus bear. The show was produced by a Moscow studio, has been dubbed into dozens of languages and some of its episodes have gathered billions of views online.
note: Describes a Russian TV/animated show.

text: Russian TV viewers have made the crime drama 'Quiet District' the most-streamed series of the autumn. Set in a small police station on the edge of a Volga town, the eight-episode show mixes slow detective work with dark humour. Critics in Moscow praised the soundtrack and the grey, rainy cinematography, and a second season has already been announced by the streaming platform.
note: Describes a (fictional) Russian TV series and its reception.

text: Every July, a rock festival on a field outside Tver draws tens of thousands of fans from across Russia. The three-day line-up mixes veteran Russian rock bands with younger indie and post-punk groups singing in Russian. Fans camp in tents, queue for shashlik, and the traditional finale is a mass sing-along of old rock anthems as fireworks go up over the main stage.
note: Describes Russian music and a music festival.

text: Russian-language rap grew from a niche underground scene in the early 2000s into the country's most popular music genre. Streaming charts in Russia are now dominated by hip-hop artists who mix trap beats with melancholic lyrics about provincial life. Many record at home and release tracks directly on VK and Yandex Music without a label, and concert tours sell out arenas across the country.
note: Describes the Russian rap music scene.

text: The Hollywood thriller 'Red Ledger' follows two deep-cover Russian agents posing as a suburban couple in Virginia. Directed by an American filmmaker and shot in Atlanta, the film stars a British and an Australian actor with carefully rehearsed accents. Critics praised the tense dinner-party scenes but noted that the plot borrows heavily from older Cold War spy dramas.
note: An American film about Russian spies: involves Russia, but it is not Russian entertainment.

text: The Odesa International Film Festival opened on Saturday with a Ukrainian comedy about a family running a seaside guesthouse. This year's programme includes twelve Ukrainian feature films, a section of short documentaries and open-air screenings at the Potemkin Stairs. Tickets for the closing night sold out in two hours, organisers said.
note: Ukrainian films and festival, not Russian entertainment.

text: Kazakh-language television drama is having a moment. 'Steppe Wind', a historical series about a family of horse breeders in the nineteenth century, became the most-watched show on national TV in Kazakhstan this spring. The producers filmed on location near Almaty and cast many first-time actors from rural villages to make the dialogue feel authentic.
note: Kazakh TV series; not Russian entertainment and Russia is not mentioned.

text: Russian pop singer Darya Velikanova surprised fans on Saturday by posting wedding photos from a private ceremony near Sochi. The 31-year-old star, known for her summer dance hits, wore a short white dress and married her long-time manager in front of about forty guests. Within hours the post had collected over two million likes, and Russian gossip sites rushed to identify the guests.
note: Gossip about an (invented) Russian pop singer.

text: Moscow beauty blogger Alina Ruzhova, who has more than eight million followers, announced she is taking a break from social media after a heated feud with another Russian influencer over a cosmetics collaboration. In a tearful video she said she needed time for her family. Fans flooded her comments with support, while critics accused her of staging the drama to boost her new product line.
note: About an (invented) Russian blogger/influencer.

text: Popular Russian TV presenter Igor Shestakov confirmed his divorce from his second wife after rumours circulated for weeks in the tabloids. The 52-year-old host of a long-running Saturday quiz show said the couple had separated amicably and would share custody of their two children. He also denied reports that he was leaving the channel.
note: Celebrity news about an (invented) Russian TV presenter.

text: Fans of Russian actor Pavel Orlin were relieved to hear he is recovering well after a knee operation. The actor, adored in Russia for his roles as charming rogues, posted a selfie from a Moscow clinic showing him on crutches with a thumbs-up. His agent said he will return to filming in the spring, and he thanked fans for the hundreds of flowers sent to the hospital.
note: Personal news about an (invented) Russian actor; not about his films.

text: Ukrainian singer Oksana Lyvynenko announced a charity tour across Western Europe, with all proceeds going to rebuild schools in the Kharkiv region. Known for her folk-pop ballads sung in Ukrainian, she will perform in Berlin, Vienna, Kraków and Lisbon. She told reporters that the new album was recorded in a small studio in Lviv during the winter.
note: An (invented) Ukrainian singer; not a Russian celebrity and Russia is not mentioned.

text: Belarusian lifestyle blogger Yana Kaval, who lives in Warsaw, has become one of the most followed creators among young Belarusians abroad. Her videos about cooking on a budget, learning Polish and decorating a tiny rented flat regularly get hundreds of thousands of views. She says she wants to show that starting over in a new country can be done with humour.
note: An (invented) Belarusian blogger; not Russian.

text: Kazakh singer Dimash Kudaibergen, famous for his extraordinary vocal range, filled an arena in Astana with a homecoming concert on Saturday. Fans from more than forty countries travelled to see him perform songs in Kazakh, English and Italian. The show featured a children's choir from his native Aktobe and a dombra ensemble.
note: A Kazakh celebrity; Russia is not involved.

text: Maslenitsa, the Russian week-long festival that marks the end of winter, is all about blini. Families fry stacks of thin pancakes and eat them with sour cream, honey, jam or red caviar. In towns across Russia there are sledging contests, folk games and, on the last day, a straw figure of Lady Winter is burned in a bonfire. The final Sunday is called Forgiveness Sunday.
note: Describes a Russian holiday tradition and food.

text: For millions of Russians, summer means the dacha. On Friday evenings city families drive out to small wooden houses with vegetable plots, where they grow potatoes, cucumbers and dill, make jam from garden berries and pickle everything they can for the winter. Weekends end with tea from a samovar or a barbecue, and with a long traffic jam back into the city on Sunday night.
note: Describes the Russian dacha way of life.

text: A Russian banya is more than a sauna. Bathers sit in a hot, humid steam room and are gently beaten with bundles of birch or oak leaves called venik to improve circulation. Between rounds they plunge into cold water or roll in snow, then rest with herbal tea. In Russia, going to the banya with friends on a Saturday is a social ritual as much as a way to get clean.
note: Describes a Russian bathing tradition.

text: New Year's Eve is the biggest family holiday in Russia. Tables are loaded with Olivier salad, herring under a fur coat and mandarins, and the champagne is opened when the Kremlin clock strikes midnight on television. Children wait for Ded Moroz and his granddaughter Snegurochka to bring presents, and many families keep the decorated tree up until mid-January.
note: Describes Russian New Year traditions and food (the Kremlin clock is a TV ritual, not politics).

text: In 2022 UNESCO added the culture of Ukrainian borscht cooking to its list of intangible heritage in need of urgent safeguarding. Every region of Ukraine has its own version: with beans in Poltava, with smoked pears in the west, with fish in the south. Recipes are passed between generations, and the dish is served with garlic pampushky and a spoon of sour cream.
note: Ukrainian food tradition, not Russian.

text: On Holy Saturday, Polish families carry decorated baskets to church to have their Easter food blessed. The święconka basket usually holds painted eggs, bread, salt, a piece of sausage, horseradish and a small lamb made of sugar or butter. The blessed food is eaten at Easter Sunday breakfast, which begins with sharing an egg and exchanging wishes.
note: Polish tradition; Russia is not involved.

text: A Georgian supra is a feast led by a tamada, the toastmaster, who proposes a long series of toasts to peace, to the ancestors, to parents, to friends and to the guests. Tables are covered with khachapuri, pkhali, grilled meat and bottles of Kakheti wine. A supra can last many hours, and polyphonic singing often breaks out between the toasts.
note: Georgian tradition; not Russian.

text: Dostoevsky's 'Crime and Punishment' follows Rodion Raskolnikov, a poor former student in St. Petersburg who murders a pawnbroker to test his theory that extraordinary people may step over moral law. Most of the novel takes place after the crime, in his feverish mind, as guilt, illness and the patient investigator Porfiry slowly break him down. It remains one of the central works of Russian literature.
note: Discusses a classic Russian novel.

text: Pushkin's 'Eugene Onegin' is a novel in verse written in a special fourteen-line stanza that the poet invented for it. Its bored, worldly hero rejects the sincere love of young Tatyana, kills his friend Lensky in a duel, and years later falls for Tatyana when she is married and refuses him. Russian readers often call it an encyclopedia of Russian life.
note: Discusses a classic work of Russian literature.

text: Andrei Rublev's icon of the Trinity, painted in the early fifteenth century and now kept in the Tretyakov Gallery in Moscow, is considered the high point of medieval Russian art. Three angels sit around a table, their bodies forming a gentle circle, in clear blues and golden ochres. Art historians admire how Rublev turned a crowded Old Testament scene into a calm image of harmony.
note: Discusses a famous work of Russian art.

text: This year's Big Book prize, Russia's best-known literary award, went to a debut novel about three generations of women in a Ural mining town. Critics praised its spare, unsentimental prose and the way it moves between the 1970s and today. The author, a former schoolteacher from Yekaterinburg, said she wrote most of the book at night after her children were asleep.
note: About contemporary Russian literature and a Russian literary prize.

text: Olga Tokarczuk's 'Flights' is a fragmented Polish novel made of short stories, essays and travel notes about bodies, movement and restlessness. One thread follows the heart of Chopin being smuggled back to Warsaw in a jar; another follows a woman who disappears on a Croatian island. The book won the International Booker Prize in its English translation.
note: A Polish novel; not Russian literature.

text: Lesya Ukrainka's verse drama 'The Forest Song' tells the story of Mavka, a forest spirit who falls in love with a young village musician, Lukash. Drawing on folklore from Volhynia, the play contrasts the free, magical world of the forest with the narrow practical life of the village. It is one of the most loved works of Ukrainian literature and is studied in every school.
note: Ukrainian literature, not Russian.

text: Alphonse Mucha's 'Slav Epic' is a cycle of twenty huge canvases painted between 1910 and 1928, depicting the mythology and history of the Czechs and other Slavic peoples. After decades rolled up in storage, the paintings are now exhibited in Prague. Visitors are often overwhelmed by their size: some are six metres high and eight metres wide.
note: Czech art; the paragraph does not discuss Russian art and Russia is not mentioned.

text: Renting a one-bedroom flat in Moscow now costs on average around 70,000 roubles a month, while outside the centre prices start near 45,000. In St. Petersburg the same flat is roughly a third cheaper. Landlords usually ask for a deposit equal to one month's rent plus an agency fee, and utilities add another 5,000 to 7,000 roubles in winter.
note: About rent and housing costs in Russia.

text: Salaries in Russia vary enormously by region. A nurse in Moscow may earn about 90,000 roubles a month, while a nurse in a small town in the Kurgan or Ivanovo region often takes home less than 40,000. Many families in the provinces rely on two jobs or on vegetables from the garden to make ends meet, and young people move to the capital mainly for the wages.
note: About salaries and making ends meet in Russia.

text: Shoppers in Russian supermarkets say their weekly basket has become noticeably more expensive. Over the past year butter has risen by about a third, and potatoes, eggs and cucumbers have also jumped in price. Pensioners interviewed in Novosibirsk said they now buy chicken instead of beef and compare receipts between stores to find the cheapest milk.
note: About grocery prices for households in Russia.

text: What does a month of everyday life cost in Kazan? Our reader, a student, shares her budget: 18,000 roubles for a shared room, 9,000 for food, 1,500 for a public transport pass, 600 for mobile internet and about 3,000 for cafés and the cinema. She works part-time in a bookshop for 25,000 a month, with the rest coming from her parents.
note: A personal budget for living in a Russian city.

text: Prices in Almaty keep climbing. A one-bedroom apartment in the Medeu district now rents for about 350,000 tenge a month, and a cappuccino in a city-centre café costs 1,500 tenge. Locals say salaries have not kept pace, and many young families are moving to the outskirts or to smaller Kazakh cities such as Shymkent, where rents are half as much.
note: Living costs in Kazakhstan, not Russia.

text: From 1 June, households in Kyiv will pay a new tariff for electricity, the government announced. The price per kilowatt-hour rises by about 60 percent, although families that use little power will receive subsidies. Energy companies say the money is needed to repair power stations and grid equipment damaged over the winter.
note: Utility costs in Ukraine; Russia is not mentioned.

text: Gazprom reported a sharp fall in quarterly net profit, citing lower export volumes to Europe and higher taxes on gas production. The company's revenue dropped by 18 percent compared with the same period last year, and its shares slipped 3 percent on the Moscow Exchange after the announcement. Analysts expect the company to cut its dividend again.
note: Russian corporate results and stock market: economy_business, not household living costs.

text: In October 1917 the Bolsheviks led by Vladimir Lenin seized power in Petrograd, overthrowing the Provisional Government that had ruled since the fall of the tsar in February. A bloody civil war followed between the Red Army and the Whites, which lasted until the early 1920s. In 1922 the Bolsheviks founded the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics.
note: Describes the founding events of Soviet history.

text: On 26 April 1986 reactor number four of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant in Soviet Ukraine exploded during a safety test. Soviet authorities delayed informing the public, and the town of Pripyat was evacuated only the next day. Radioactive fallout spread across Ukraine, Belarus and much of Europe, and the disaster deeply damaged trust in the Soviet leadership.
note: Describes an event of Soviet history.

text: In May 1944 Soviet security forces deported almost the entire Crimean Tatar population to Central Asia on Stalin's orders, accusing them collectively of collaboration with Nazi Germany. Tens of thousands died on the journey or in the first years of exile. Crimean Tatars were not allowed to return to Crimea until the late 1980s.
note: Describes Soviet-era deportations; historical, not a narrative.

text: On 8 December 1991 the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus met in the Belovezha Forest and signed an agreement declaring that the Soviet Union had ceased to exist. Two weeks later most of the remaining republics joined the new Commonwealth of Independent States, and on 25 December Mikhail Gorbachev resigned as Soviet president. The red flag was lowered over the Kremlin that evening.
note: Describes the end of the USSR in 1991.

text: In October 1993 a constitutional crisis in Moscow ended in violence when President Boris Yeltsin ordered tanks to shell the parliament building, the White House, after deputies tried to remove him from office. Dozens of people were killed. Two months later Russians approved a new constitution that gave the president far greater powers than the legislature.
note: Post-1991 Russian politics, not Soviet history.

text: Vladimir Putin was first elected president of Russia in March 2000 after serving as acting president following Boris Yeltsin's surprise resignation on New Year's Eve. His first term brought a centralisation of power: regional governors lost their seats in the upper house, and independent television channels came under state control.
note: Post-Soviet Russian politics; not about Soviet history.

text: In August 1980 workers at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk went on strike after a crane operator was fired. Led by electrician Lech Wałęsa, they formed Solidarity, the first independent trade union in the communist bloc. Within a year it had nearly ten million members, until martial law was declared in Poland in December 1981.
note: Polish communist-era history; the USSR and Russia are not referred to (the shipyard name is a keyword only).

text: CSKA Moscow beat SKA St. Petersburg 3-2 in overtime on Tuesday to level the KHL conference final at two games each. The winning goal came after four minutes of extra time from a rebound in front of the net. The Moscow side had trailed 2-0 after the first period but turned the game around with two power-play goals.
note: About Russian hockey teams.

text: Russian figure skater Ksenia Morozova, 16, landed two quadruple jumps in her free programme to win the national championship in Chelyabinsk. Her score of 245 points was the highest in the country this season. Her coach said the team will now focus on improving her spins and artistry before next season's domestic Grand Prix events.
note: About an (invented) Russian athlete.

text: Zenit St. Petersburg have clinched the Russian Premier League title for another season after a 2-0 win against Krasnodar. The St. Petersburg club secured the trophy with two rounds to spare, thanks mainly to its Brazilian forwards and the league's best defence. Fans celebrated on Nevsky Prospekt late into the night.
note: About a Russian football club.

text: Russian tennis player Daniil Medvedev, competing as a neutral athlete, reached the quarter-finals after a four-set win in nearly three and a half hours. The former US Open champion struggled with his serve early on but took control with long baseline rallies. He will face a seeded Italian opponent in the next round.
note: About a Russian athlete's match.

text: Ukrainian boxer Oleksandr Usyk defended his heavyweight titles with a unanimous decision victory in London. Using his footwork and speed, the southpaw outboxed his taller opponent over twelve rounds. After the fight Usyk dedicated the win to his family and to Ukraine, and said he wants to fight at least two more times before retiring.
note: A Ukrainian athlete; Russia is not involved.

text: The Kazakh professional cycling team Astana finished the Tour de France with two stage wins and a top-ten place in the general classification. The team, sponsored by Kazakhstan's sovereign wealth fund, has relied on a mix of experienced European riders and young Kazakh talents. Its manager said the mountain stages were the highlight of the race.
note: A Kazakh sports team; not Russian.

text: The Tampa Bay Rays beat the New York Yankees 5-3 on Saturday night at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida. A two-run homer in the seventh inning gave the Rays the lead, and the bullpen held on for the final three innings. The win moves the team within two games of first place in the AL East.
note: US baseball in St. Petersburg, Florida; no Russian sport or Russia.

text: CatBoost is an open-source gradient boosting library developed by engineers at Yandex in Moscow and released in 2017. Its main innovation is ordered boosting, which reduces target leakage when encoding categorical features. The library handles categorical columns natively, trains on CPU or GPU, and ships with Python, R and command-line interfaces.
note: Describes software developed in Russia; no company/market focus.

text: Researchers at the Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology near Moscow have reported a new cathode material for lithium-ion batteries based on a modified iron phosphate structure. In laboratory tests the cells kept 92 percent of their capacity after 2,000 charge cycles. The team says the material avoids cobalt entirely and could be produced with existing equipment.
note: Reports a technology developed by a Russian research institute.

text: Nginx began as a side project of Igor Sysoev, a system administrator in Moscow, who wanted a web server that could handle ten thousand simultaneous connections. Instead of one thread per connection, nginx uses an asynchronous, event-driven architecture with a small number of worker processes. Today it is widely used as a reverse proxy, load balancer and HTTP cache.
note: Explains software developed in Russia and how it works.

text: The Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions in Dubna, Russia, is known for synthesising superheavy elements. Physicists there bombard heavy actinide targets with beams of calcium-48 ions and detect the short-lived nuclei by their decay chains. Element 114, flerovium, is named after the laboratory, and the method has been used to produce elements up to 118.
note: Explains a scientific method developed at a Russian laboratory.

text: At an international machine learning conference in Moscow, several speakers cited the transformer architecture, first described in 2017 by a Google research team in California. One session compared attention variants on long documents, while another asked whether the original design is still the best default. Slides from the event were posted online after the conference.
note: Russia is only the conference venue; the technology discussed was developed in the US.

text: Grammarly was founded in 2009 by three engineers who had studied in Kyiv, and much of its early development took place in Ukraine. The writing assistant combines rule-based grammar checks with machine learning models that suggest clearer wording. The company now has offices in Kyiv, San Francisco and Vancouver and serves millions of users.
note: Technology developed in Ukraine/US; Russia is not mentioned.

text: Wargaming, the studio behind World of Tanks, was founded in Minsk, Belarus, in 1998. Its engineers built a custom client-server architecture that lets tens of thousands of players fight in parallel battles with low latency. In 2022 the company closed its Minsk office and moved its main development to studios in other European countries.
note: Technology developed in Belarus, not Russia; no Russian reference.

text: The Volga is the longest river in Europe, flowing about 3,530 kilometres through western Russia. It rises in the Valdai Hills northwest of Moscow and empties into the Caspian Sea near Astrakhan, forming a wide delta. Its drainage basin covers roughly 1.36 million square kilometres, and a chain of reservoirs regulates much of its course.
note: Describes a Russian river's length, course and basin.

text: Lake Baikal in southern Siberia is the deepest lake on Earth, reaching 1,642 metres at its deepest point. It lies in a rift valley between the Irkutsk region and the Republic of Buryatia and holds about a fifth of the world's unfrozen fresh surface water. More than 300 rivers flow into it, but only one, the Angara, flows out.
note: Describes physical geography of a lake in Russia.

text: Russia and Kazakhstan share a land border of about 7,600 kilometres, one of the longest continuous international borders in the world. It runs from the Caspian Sea in the west, across the steppes south of the Ural Mountains, to the Altai Mountains in the east, where the borders of Russia, Kazakhstan, China and Mongolia come close together.
note: Describes the length and course of a Russian border.

text: Q: How far is it from Moscow to Vladivostok by train? A: The main Trans-Siberian route is about 9,289 km and crosses seven time zones. Without stops it takes roughly six days. By air the distance is around 6,400 km. Most of the line runs through southern Siberia, close to the borders with Kazakhstan, Mongolia and China.
note: Gives distances and route geography within Russia.

text: Stayed three nights at a hotel near Tverskaya Street in Moscow. The room was small but spotless, the bed was comfortable and the staff at reception spoke good English. Breakfast had a decent choice of eggs, pastries and fruit. Wi-Fi dropped a couple of times in the evening. Would stay again, but ask for a room facing the courtyard because the street side is noisy.
note: Hotel review set in Moscow; says nothing about geography, borders or distances.

text: Moscow, Idaho, sits on the Palouse, a region of rolling wheat-covered hills in the northern part of the state. The city lies about 8 miles east of Pullman, Washington, across the state line, and roughly 90 miles south of Coeur d'Alene. Paradise Creek runs through town, and Moscow Mountain rises to the northeast.
note: Geography of Moscow, Idaho, not Russia; incidental keyword.

text: The Ukrainian Carpathians stretch for about 280 kilometres across the west of the country. The highest peak, Hoverla, reaches 2,061 metres in the Chornohora range. The mountains are the source of the Tisza and Prut rivers, and their beech and spruce forests make up one of the most heavily wooded areas of Ukraine.
note: Geography of Ukraine; Russia is not mentioned.

text: The State Duma has passed in its third reading a bill that widens the definition of a "foreign agent" in Russia. Under the new rules, a person can be added to the registry if they are judged to be "under foreign influence", even without receiving money from abroad. Those listed will be barred from teaching in state schools and from running for public office.
note: Reports on a Russian law passed by the Duma.

text: The 2020 amendments to the Russian Constitution were approved in a nationwide vote held over several days in late June and early July. Among other changes, they reset the count of presidential terms for the sitting president, allowing Vladimir Putin to run again in 2024 and 2030. Critics pointed to the unusual voting procedure and the lack of independent observers.
note: About Russian constitutional changes and the president.

text: Russia holds most regional and municipal elections on a single voting day in September. This year governors were chosen in more than twenty regions, and in almost every case the incumbent appointed by the Kremlin as acting governor won with a large majority. Election officials reported that online voting was available in several regions for the first time.
note: About Russian regional elections and governors.

text: Russia's Ministry of Finance has proposed raising the profit tax for large companies from 20 to 25 percent starting next January. Finance Minister Anton Siluanov told lawmakers that the extra revenue is needed to balance the federal budget. The bill also introduces a progressive personal income tax scale for the first time since 2001.
note: About a Russian government tax policy and its minister.

text: Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko has signed a decree reorganising the country's regional administrations in Minsk, Gomel and Brest. The changes merge several district committees and transfer some powers to regional governors. The government in Minsk says the reform will cut administrative costs by about 15 percent.
note: Belarusian government, not Russian; no reference to Russia.

text: The Russian Chess Club of Toronto held its annual meeting on Saturday and elected a new five-member board. Members voted to move the weekly blitz evenings to Thursdays and to raise the junior membership fee slightly. The outgoing chair thanked volunteers who helped organise last spring's open tournament for players of all ages.
note: A diaspora club's internal election; not about the Russian government.

text: The Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine approved a law on electronic public procurement that requires all municipal tenders above a set threshold to be published on the Prozorro platform. Deputies from several factions supported the bill, which also introduces fines for officials who split contracts to avoid open bidding.
note: Ukrainian parliament and policy; Russia not mentioned.

text: Russian forces launched dozens of missiles and attack drones at Ukraine overnight, targeting power plants and substations in the Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk and Lviv regions. Ukraine's air force said most of the drones were shot down. Emergency power cuts were introduced in several cities, and officials reported that two people were killed in Kharkiv.
note: Reports a Russian strike on Ukraine.

text: In September 2022 Ukrainian forces launched a rapid counteroffensive in the Kharkiv region. Within days they broke through Russian lines near Balakliia and advanced toward Kupiansk and Izium, recapturing thousands of square kilometres. Russian units withdrew across the Oskil River, leaving behind large amounts of equipment.
note: Reports a phase of Russia's war against Ukraine.

text: Ukrainian naval drones have struck several ships of Russia's Black Sea Fleet since the full-scale invasion began. After repeated attacks near Sevastopol, much of the fleet was moved to Novorossiysk, further from the front. Military analysts say the losses allowed Ukraine to reopen a shipping corridor for grain exports from Odesa.
note: Reports naval events in Russia's war against Ukraine.

text: According to UN figures, more than six million refugees from Ukraine have been recorded across Europe since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. Poland, Germany and the Czech Republic host the largest numbers. Millions more people remain internally displaced inside Ukraine, many of them from towns near the front line in the east.
note: Reports humanitarian consequences of Russia's war against Ukraine.

text: In the autumn of 2016, Syrian government forces, backed by Russian aircraft, tightened the siege of eastern Aleppo. Rebel-held neighbourhoods were cut off from supplies, and hospitals in the area were repeatedly hit. By December the remaining fighters and tens of thousands of civilians were evacuated in green buses to Idlib province.
note: Russia is involved, but the war is in Syria, not against Ukraine.

text: The Battle of Kyiv in the summer of 1941 ended in one of the largest encirclements in military history. German army groups closed a pocket east of the city, and the Red Army lost more than 600,000 soldiers killed or captured. Kyiv itself fell on 19 September and remained under German occupation until November 1943.
note: WWII battle in Ukraine (Soviet history), not the Russian war against Ukraine.

text: Ukraine harvested a record 75 million tonnes of grain in 2019, according to the Ministry of Agrarian Policy. Corn made up the largest share, followed by wheat and barley. Favourable weather and higher yields in the central regions helped farmers, and exporters shipped most of the surplus through the ports of Odesa and Mykolaiv.
note: Ukrainian agriculture before the full-scale war; no Russia, no war.

text: Gazprom reported a net loss for the full year, its first in more than two decades. Revenue fell sharply after pipeline gas exports to Europe collapsed, and the company's attempts to redirect volumes to China have so far offset only a small part of the drop. Analysts expect the state-controlled firm to cut its investment programme next year.
note: About a Russian company's results.

text: Trading in the Chinese yuan on the Moscow Exchange has overtaken trading in the US dollar for the first time. Russian exporters and banks have shifted to the yuan since Western sanctions restricted dollar and euro settlements. Daily turnover in the yuan-ruble pair now regularly exceeds the equivalent of several billion dollars.
note: About Russian markets and sanctions.

text: The EU's latest sanctions package targets the shadow fleet of tankers that carries Russian oil above the price cap. More than seventy vessels were added to the list, barring them from EU ports and services. The package also restricts exports of machine tools and electronic components that could reach Russian manufacturers through third countries.
note: About sanctions on Russian trade.

text: Russian online retailer Wildberries is building three new fulfilment centres in the Urals and Siberia, aiming to cut delivery times outside the Moscow region to two days. The company, which merged with outdoor advertising group Russ last year, says its number of sellers has grown by 40 percent and that it is hiring several thousand warehouse workers.
note: About a Russian company's business expansion.

text: Ukrainian logistics company Nova Poshta has opened branches in Poland, Lithuania and Moldova to serve Ukrainians living abroad. The firm says parcel volumes on international routes grew by a third last year, and it plans to launch its own cargo flights between Kyiv and European hubs once airspace reopens.
note: Ukrainian company; Russia not mentioned.

text: Sales of bottled salad dressings rose 6 percent last year at a mid-sized US food company in Ohio. Ranch remained the best seller, but Thousand Island and Russian dressing gained shelf space in supermarkets after the firm cut prices. Management expects to add a new production line in the spring.
note: Russian dressing is an incidental keyword; a US company.

text: A week of groceries in Moscow now costs a family of four noticeably more than last spring. Our basket of milk, bread, eggs, buckwheat, chicken, potatoes, apples and cheese came to about 7,800 rubles, up from 6,900. Rent for a two-room flat in a sleeping district is around 60,000 rubles a month, roughly half of an average Moscow salary.
note: Household prices and rent in Moscow: cost of living, not companies or markets.

text: Russian pop singer Alina Vereskova, known for her chart-topping dance hits, has co-founded a technology startup in Moscow. The company is developing a neural network that turns hummed melodies into full backing tracks, and its first app entered beta testing this month. The singer says she will promote it during her autumn tour.
note: Celebrity + music (remove) and Russian-developed software + startup company (keep).

text: Engineers at Baikal Electronics, the Moscow-based designer of Russian processors, earn between 250,000 and 400,000 rubles a month, according to job listings. That is well above the average salary in Moscow, but recruiters say it still lags behind what chip designers can earn abroad, and the company struggles to keep staff.
note: Salaries in Russia (remove) at a Russian company (keep).

text: The Kinotavr film festival in Sochi went ahead this year despite sanctions that cut off its Western sponsors. Organisers replaced them with Russian banks and a state-owned energy company, and the programme featured fourteen new Russian feature films. Foreign guests were few, as most international distributors no longer buy Russian titles.
note: Russian films/festival (remove) and sanctions/companies (keep).

text: Maslenitsa, the week of pancakes and bonfires before Lent, is celebrated in every town along the Yenisei, a river that flows about 3,500 kilometres north from the mountains of Tuva to the Kara Sea. In Krasnoyarsk, festivities take place on the frozen riverbank, while villages near the Arctic coast burn the straw effigy weeks before the ice breaks.
note: Russian tradition (remove) combined with river geography (keep).

text: Russia's government has approved the official calendar of public holidays for next year. The New Year holidays will again run from 1 to 8 January, covering Orthodox Christmas, and the Day of National Unity on 4 November remains a day off. The Ministry of Labour said it moved two weekend days to create longer breaks in May.
note: Government policy (keep) on Russian holidays (remove).

text: A Russian rock band performed for Russian soldiers in occupied Luhansk region last week, according to video posted by the group. The concert took place in a school gym a few dozen kilometres from the front line. Ukrainian officials said the same area had been shelled the day before, and the band's planned European tour was cancelled.
note: Russian music performance (remove) within reporting on the war (keep).

text: Rents in large Russian cities have risen by about a fifth over the past year. Economists link the increase to sanctions that pushed up construction costs and to the central bank's high key rate, which made mortgages unaffordable and kept more families renting. Developers have postponed several big housing projects in Yekaterinburg and Kazan.
note: Living costs (remove) tied to sanctions, markets and developers (keep).

text: The Saint Petersburg studio behind the action game Iron Taiga built its own rendering engine instead of licensing a Western one. The engine uses a voxel-based global illumination technique that lets thousands of trees cast dynamic shadows at playable frame rates. The game itself, a story about a hunter in Siberia, sold well among Russian players.
note: Russian video game (remove) and Russian-developed engine technology (keep).

text: Moscow Zoo has welcomed a new resident: a two-year-old red panda named Bao arrived from a zoo in the Czech Republic. Keepers say he spent the first week exploring his enclosure and has already learned to come down from the tree at feeding time. Visitors can see him in the Asian forest pavilion from Tuesday to Sunday.
note: About Russia (Moscow Zoo) but none of the 12 subjects.

text: Scheduling tip: Moscow uses UTC+3 all year and has not changed clocks since 2014. So when London switches to summer time, the gap shrinks from three hours to two. If your team in Berlin wants to call colleagues in Moscow at 10:00 their time, set the meeting for 08:00 in winter and 09:00 in summer.
note: Time-zone note about Moscow; not geography of borders/rivers/distances.

text: Staff at the main bus station in Novosibirsk have adopted a ginger cat that turned up on the platform during a snowstorm. The cat, now called Ryzhik, sleeps in the ticket office and greets passengers on the morning buses. A local vet checked him for free, and drivers have started bringing him treats from home.
note: Local human-interest story set in Russia; no listed subject.

text: Filling in the Russian e-visa form: upload a passport-style photo on a light background, enter your passport number exactly as printed, and list the cities you plan to visit. After you submit, save the PDF confirmation and print it, because border officers may ask to see it. The status page usually updates within four days.
note: Practical paperwork steps for a Russian visa; not about government policy or officials.

text: Russians and Ukrainians are one people, a single nation divided only by borders that the Bolsheviks drew on a map. There has never been a separate Ukrainian nation; Kyiv was the cradle of our common civilisation since Kievan Rus, and the same faith, language and history bind us together. The so-called Ukrainian identity was invented by Austrian and Polish intriguers to split one people, and sooner or later this artificial division will be overcome.
note: States in its own voice that Ukrainians and Russians are one people and Ukraine was never a nation.

text: Honestly, there is no such thing as a Ukrainian nation. It's the same people as the Russians: same faith, same history, same family names. A 'country' that only appeared on the map in 1991 is not a nation, it's an administrative accident. Ask anyone's grandmother in Kharkiv or Odesa and she'll tell you she is Russian like everyone else. The whole 'separate nation' story is a political project of the last thirty years, nothing more.
note: Forum post asserting Ukrainians are not a separate nation from Russians.

text: Ukrainian statehood is a fiction. Before the twentieth century nobody spoke of Ukrainians as a people; there were Little Russians, one branch of the great Russian nation alongside the Great Russians and the Belarusians. Modern Kyiv tries to build a nation by rewriting history, but a people cannot be created by decree. Russians and Ukrainians share one soul, and no border drawn by politicians can change that.
note: Op-ed claiming Ukrainians are merely a branch of one Russian nation.

text: Claim: 'Ukrainians and Russians are one people, and Ukraine was never a real nation.' Verdict: False. The claim, repeated in a 2021 essay published on the Kremlin's website, ignores centuries of distinct Ukrainian language, literature and political institutions, from the Cossack Hetmanate to the Ukrainian People's Republic of 1917. Historians note that the 'one people' framing has long been used to deny Ukrainian sovereignty.
note: Fact-check quoting and refuting the 'one people' claim; the text does not adopt it.

text: The Ukrainian national movement took shape in the nineteenth century, when writers such as Taras Shevchenko and historians like Mykhailo Hrushevsky documented the Ukrainian language, folklore and past. After the collapse of the Russian Empire, the Ukrainian People's Republic declared independence in January 1918. Ukraine later became a Soviet republic and regained full independence in 1991, confirmed by a referendum in which more than 90 percent voted in favour.
note: Neutral encyclopedic history of Ukrainian nationhood; no claim that Ukraine is not a nation.

text: The regime in Kyiv is a Nazi regime. Its battalions march under symbols borrowed from the SS, its streets are named after Hitler's collaborators, and its leaders openly worship fascist ideology. Ukraine today is the only country in Europe where Nazism has become state policy, and the West pretends not to see it. Russian people remember who defeated Nazism eighty years ago, and they recognise it again in Kyiv.
note: Asserts as fact that the Ukrainian government is Nazi.

text: Ukrainian soldiers are neo-Nazis, plain and simple. They are the grandsons of Bandera's men and they fight against Russia with the same hatred their grandfathers had. Every unit has its runes and portraits of collaborators on the walls. Whenever Russian troops enter a town abandoned by the Ukrainian army, they find Nazi literature in every barracks. This is who the West is arming.
note: Labels Ukrainian soldiers as neo-Nazis in the war context, in its own voice.

text: The Kyiv junta that seized power in 2014 is a Nazi government in all but name. It glorifies wartime collaborators, tears down monuments to the soldiers who liberated Europe and persecutes anyone who remembers the victory over fascism. Its ministers speak the language of racial purity. Russians, whose grandparents paid for that victory with millions of lives, cannot accept a neo-Nazi state on their border.
note: Calls the Ukrainian government Nazi as its own claim.

text: Russian President Vladimir Putin again claimed on Tuesday that Ukraine's government is run by 'neo-Nazis', repeating a justification he has used since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022. Ukrainian officials rejected the remark, pointing out that President Volodymyr Zelensky is Jewish and was elected with 73 percent of the vote. Far-right parties won about 2 percent in Ukraine's 2019 parliamentary election.
note: News report quoting and contextualising the Nazi claim without adopting it.

text: The Azov unit was formed in 2014 as a volunteer battalion and was later incorporated into Ukraine's National Guard. Its early ranks included members of far-right groups, which drew criticism from human rights organisations at the time. The unit has since been reorganised, and it became widely known for defending the Azovstal steel plant in Mariupol during the Russian siege of the city in spring 2022.
note: Neutral factual paragraph on a topic often used in the Nazi narrative; makes no such claim.

text: The special military operation was never an act of aggression. Russia was forced to step in to protect the people of Donbas, who had been shelled for eight years while the world looked away. Our soldiers are liberating towns, not conquering them, and residents greet them as defenders. Every country has the right to defend its own people, and that is exactly what Russia is doing.
note: Frames the invasion as a defensive, liberating special operation.

text: Moscow, 14 March. The Russian Armed Forces continue the special military operation to demilitarise Ukraine and protect the civilian population of Donbas. Thanks to the courageous actions of our servicemen, three more settlements have been liberated from nationalist formations, and their residents are already receiving humanitarian aid. The operation is proceeding strictly according to plan, and all its objectives will be achieved.
note: State-media style bulletin adopting the 'liberation / special operation' framing as its own.

text: People keep calling it an invasion, but Russia had no choice. Kyiv was massing troops for an offensive on Donbas and, with Western weapons, would have attacked Russia itself next. Striking first was self-defence, pure and simple. If Russia had waited a few more months, the war would now be fought on its own territory, in its own cities. The operation saved lives on both sides.
note: Forum post presenting the invasion as pre-emptive self-defence.

text: Moscow describes its invasion as a 'special military operation' to protect Donbas residents and 'demilitarise' Ukraine. The UN General Assembly rejected that framing in March 2022, when 141 states voted to condemn the invasion as an act of aggression. The International Court of Justice also ordered Russia to suspend its military operations, noting it had no evidence for the genocide allegations Moscow used to justify them.
note: Reports the justification and the international rejection of it; does not adopt it.

text: On 24 February 2022 Russian forces launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine from the north, east and south, including from Belarusian territory. Columns advanced towards Kyiv but withdrew from the region at the end of March. Fighting then concentrated in the east and south, where Ukraine recaptured large areas around Kharkiv and Kherson in the autumn before front lines largely stabilised in 2023.
note: Neutral factual account of the invasion with no justification.

text: This war is NATO's war. For thirty years the alliance crept eastward, breaking every promise made to Moscow, until it stood at Russia's doorstep. Washington armed Ukraine and pushed it into confrontation, knowing exactly how Russia would respond. The blame for every death on this front lies in Brussels and Washington, not in Moscow. The West wanted this war and it got it.
note: Blames NATO and the West for causing the war.

text: The West started this conflict in 2014 when it organised a coup in Kyiv and installed a puppet government. Since then American and British advisers have trained, armed and directed the Ukrainian army. Ukraine is only a battering ram; the real enemy of peace is the Anglo-Saxon elite that wants to weaken and dismember Russia at any price, using Ukrainian lives as currency.
note: Claims the West orchestrated the conflict to weaken Russia.

text: Without NATO expansion there would be no war. Every serious analyst knew that pulling Ukraine into the Western bloc was a red line for Russia, and the Americans said so themselves in the 1990s. The West crossed that line anyway and now pretends to be surprised. The responsibility for this war belongs to those who ignored Russia's warnings for decades, not to Russia.
note: Blog asserting NATO expansion caused the war.

text: Speaking in Brussels, NATO's Secretary General rejected Russian claims that the alliance had provoked the war, saying NATO is a defensive alliance and that Ukraine is a sovereign nation with the right to choose its own path. Moscow has repeatedly argued that NATO enlargement forced its hand, an argument that many security analysts describe as a pretext for a war of conquest.
note: News piece reporting and rebutting the NATO-blame claim.

text: NATO expanded in several waves after the end of the Cold War. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic joined in 1999, followed in 2004 by seven more countries, including Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. Finland became a member in April 2023 and Sweden in March 2024. Finland's accession more than doubled the length of the alliance's land border with Russia, adding about 1,340 kilometres.
note: Neutral facts about NATO enlargement; no blame for the war.

text: Crimea is Russian and always will be. The peninsula returned home in 2014, when its people voted overwhelmingly to reunite with Russia, correcting the historical mistake Khrushchev made when he handed it to Ukraine in 1954. Sevastopol is a city of Russian glory, and the question of Crimea is closed forever. No sanctions and no Western resolutions will ever change that.
note: Asserts Crimea belongs to Russia.

text: The Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions are now part of the Russian Federation, as their residents decided in the referendums of 2022. These are Russian lands inhabited by Russian people, and their return to Russia is final and irreversible. Any talk of 'occupied territories' is simply Western propaganda; there is nothing occupied about a region that has come home.
note: Claims the occupied regions legitimately belong to Russia.

text: Planning a summer trip to the Russian Black Sea coast? Don't forget Crimea, Russia's favourite holiday region! Since the peninsula rejoined the Russian Federation, Sevastopol and Yalta have new roads, renovated promenades and a bridge linking them to the rest of the country. Crimea is part of Russia, so all you need is your internal passport and a good pair of sandals.
note: Travel-blog style text that presents Crimea as part of Russia as a matter of course.

text: Russia claims to have annexed four Ukrainian regions after so-called referendums held in September 2022 under military occupation. The UN General Assembly declared the votes invalid, with 143 countries supporting the resolution. Kyiv and its allies say the territories remain part of Ukraine under international law, and independent observers reported that residents were pressured to vote in front of armed soldiers.
note: Reports the annexation claim critically; does not adopt it.

text: Crimea is a peninsula on the northern coast of the Black Sea, connected to the mainland by the narrow Perekop Isthmus. Its southern coast is sheltered by the Crimean Mountains, whose highest peak, Roman-Kosh, rises to 1,545 metres. The climate ranges from dry steppe in the north to a mild, almost subtropical belt along the shore between Alushta and Yalta.
note: Neutral geography of Crimea; says nothing about whom it belongs to and does not mention Russia.

text: The so-called Bucha massacre was a staged provocation. Russian troops left the town days before the bodies appeared, and the footage was carefully arranged for Western cameras. It is the same script every time: fake bodies, fake witnesses, and a ready-made story in all the Western media within hours. Anyone who looks at the timeline honestly can see it was a performance.
note: Claims the Bucha killings were staged.

text: The strike on the maternity hospital in Mariupol never happened the way Western media reported it. The building had long been taken over by Ukrainian fighters, and the 'pregnant women' in the photos were hired actors. Russian forces do not target civilians; these stories are invented in Kyiv to turn the world against Russia and to beg for more weapons.
note: Denies a documented attack and calls victims actors.

text: Every 'war crime' attributed to the Russian army turns out to be Ukrainian theatre. Mass graves, deported children, mistreated prisoners: all of it is fabricated by Kyiv's propaganda ministry and paid for with Western money. Not one of these accusations would survive an honest, independent investigation, which is exactly why the West never allows one.
note: Blanket claim that documented Russian war crimes are fabricated.

text: Russian officials have claimed that images of dead civilians in Bucha were 'staged' after Russian forces withdrew. Satellite images published by Maxar Technologies, however, show bodies lying in the streets in mid-March 2022, while the town was still under Russian control. UN investigators and journalists later documented unlawful killings there, contradicting the Kremlin's version of events.
note: Fact-check quoting the denial and refuting it.

text: In March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin and Russia's children's rights commissioner, Maria Lvova-Belova, over the unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children from occupied territories. Ukraine has identified around 20,000 children it says were taken to Russia. Russia does not recognise the court's jurisdiction, and the warrants restrict where its president can travel.
note: Neutral report on war-crime proceedings; no denial.

text: Ukrainian is not a real language. It is a regional dialect of Russian mixed with Polish words, given a written standard only in the nineteenth century by a handful of intellectuals. Anyone from Moscow can understand it without any study. Forcing this dialect on schools, courts and offices is an artificial political project designed to push people away from Russia.
note: States Ukrainian is a dialect of Russian, not a language.

text: Let's be honest, the 'Ukrainian language' is just Little Russian peasant speech that intellectuals dressed up with Polish grammar and invented words. Real literature, science and business in Kyiv were always conducted in Russian. Calling a village dialect a separate language was a political decision, not a linguistic one, and everyone who grew up there knows it.
note: Forum post dismissing Ukrainian as a dressed-up dialect.

text: In our school we teach children the truth: there is one great Russian language with three branches, Great Russian, Little Russian and Belarusian. The so-called Ukrainian language is simply the Little Russian dialect, artificially separated from its root by politicians. When a dialect is taught as if it were a foreign language, children lose their connection to real Russian culture.
note: Teacher's statement that Ukrainian is a dialect of Russian.

text: Is Ukrainian just a dialect of Russian? No. Linguists classify Ukrainian as a separate East Slavic language with its own grammar, phonetics and vocabulary; in shared vocabulary it is closer to Belarusian and Polish than to Russian. The 'dialect' claim goes back to the Russian Empire, whose 1863 Valuev Circular declared that a separate Little Russian language 'never existed and cannot exist'.
note: Fact-check quoting and debunking the dialect claim.

text: Ukrainian is the state language of Ukraine and is spoken by roughly 30 to 40 million people. It is written in a Cyrillic alphabet of 33 letters, including Ґ, Є, І and Ї. Together with Russian and Belarusian, it belongs to the East Slavic branch of the Slavic languages. Its literary standard is based mainly on the dialects of the central Dnipro region.
note: Neutral linguistic facts; Russian is mentioned only as a language in a list, so the gate is false.

text: Russia is not just a country, it is a civilisation. From the Baltic to the Pacific, Russian power has united dozens of peoples under one great state, and every attempt by the West to break it has ended in defeat. The Russian world lives wherever the Russian language and the Orthodox faith are alive, and its destiny is to remain a great power that others must respect.
note: Glorifies Russian power and the 'Russian world'.

text: Peter the Great and Catherine the Great built an empire that made all of Europe tremble. Russia's glory has always rested on its strength: the strength to master endless lands, to crush Napoleon and to stand alone against the whole world. Today the Russian world is rising again, and those who doubted it will soon remember what a great empire means.
note: Celebrates Russian imperial might and its revival.

text: The Russian world is our home. Wherever Russians live, in Riga, in Almaty or in Odesa, they belong to one great civilisation whose heart is Moscow. Our duty is to keep it united and strong. No other nation has given humanity such a spirit, such a culture and such strength, and no other nation has been chosen by history for so great a mission.
note: Promotes 'Russian world' supremacy in its own voice.

text: The concept of the 'Russian world' (russkiy mir) has become a central element of Kremlin ideology. Critics argue that it presents Russian-speaking communities abroad as part of a single civilisation led by Moscow, which provides a pretext for interference in neighbouring states. In 2022 hundreds of Orthodox theologians signed a declaration rejecting the 'Russian world' teaching as incompatible with their faith.
note: Critical analysis of the 'Russian world' doctrine, not an endorsement.

text: The Russian Empire reached its greatest territorial extent in the 1860s, covering about 22.8 million square kilometres across Eastern Europe, Central Asia and Siberia, as well as Alaska, which was sold to the United States in 1867. The empire was ruled by the Romanov dynasty until the February Revolution of 1917 forced Nicholas II to abdicate.
note: Neutral historical facts about imperial size without glorification.

text: Life in the USSR was better, and everyone who lived then knows it. Housing was free, education and medicine were free, and nobody was afraid of tomorrow. The peoples of fifteen republics lived as one big family. The collapse of the Soviet Union was the greatest tragedy of the century, and one day our great country will be restored.
note: Praises the USSR and hopes for its restoration.

text: Born in the USSR and proud of it! Our Soviet Union defeated fascism, sent the first man into space and built a fair society without oligarchs. Today's leaders could learn a lot from Stalin about order and discipline. People were honest, the factories worked and everyone had a job. Bring back the Union, because the people want it.
note: Nostalgic praise of the USSR and a call to bring it back.

text: We must restore the Soviet Union in a new form. Russia, Belarus, Ukraine and Kazakhstan belong together, as they did for seventy years under the red flag. The Soviet system gave us industrial might and social justice that no market economy has ever matched. The day the Union is reborn will be the day of our true victory.
note: Calls for restoring the USSR and praises its system.

text: According to a recent Levada Center poll, around two thirds of Russians say they regret the collapse of the Soviet Union, most often citing the loss of a common economic system and of the feeling of belonging to a great power. Sociologists caution that such nostalgia usually reflects dissatisfaction with present-day conditions rather than a genuine wish to restore the Soviet system.
note: Reports survey opinions and analyses them; the text itself does not praise the USSR.

text: The Soviet Union was formally dissolved on 26 December 1991, a day after Mikhail Gorbachev resigned as its president. Its fifteen republics became independent states, and Russia took over the Soviet seat on the UN Security Council. The Commonwealth of Independent States, founded earlier that month, was intended to manage the transition between the former republics.
note: Neutral account of the Soviet collapse.

text: Ukrainians are like a herd of sheep. They follow whoever feeds them, yesterday Russia, today the Americans, tomorrow someone else. A people with no spine and no brain, good only for begging and grabbing what belongs to others. Russia fed them for decades and this is the thanks it gets. Nothing a Ukrainian says can ever be trusted.
note: Dehumanising generalisation about Ukrainians as a people.

text: They are not like us. Ukrainians are a sick, degenerate people, rotten from the inside, a parasite that lives on Western handouts the same way it once lived on cheap Russian gas. You cannot reason with such creatures, and you should not waste your pity on them. Whatever happens to them, they brought it on themselves.
note: Calls Ukrainians parasites and creatures.

text: Every time I read the news from Kyiv I am reminded that Ukrainians are vermin who spread wherever there is something to grab. Half of Europe is now infested with them, and the Europeans are only starting to notice. Russians tried for centuries to treat them as brothers, but you cannot make a brother out of a rat.
note: Vermin / infestation language about Ukrainians.

text: A study by a media monitoring group found that Russian state television regularly described Ukrainians as 'vermin' and 'a sick nation' during prime-time talk shows in 2022. The researchers counted hundreds of such remarks and warned that dehumanising language about an entire people often precedes and accompanies mass violence against civilians.
note: Reports and condemns dehumanising speech; does not use it in its own voice.

text: According to the 2001 census, the only one held since independence, Ukraine had a population of about 48.5 million. Ethnic Ukrainians made up roughly 78 percent, and Russians, the largest minority, about 17 percent, living mostly in the east, the south and Crimea. Smaller communities included Belarusians, Moldovans, Crimean Tatars, Bulgarians, Hungarians and Poles.
note: Neutral demographic facts about Ukrainians; no hostility.

text: Russians are not a nation but a horde. For centuries they have lived like locusts, devouring everything around them and leaving only ruins behind. There is something broken in them as a people: they love their chains and hate anyone who is free. The world will only be safe when this barbarian mass is shut away behind a wall.
note: Dehumanises Russians as a people (horde, locusts, barbarian mass).

text: Talking to Russians is pointless. They are a slave people, bred for obedience, a grey crowd without conscience or memory. Like animals they recognise only force and the hand that feeds them. Every Russian, from the soldier to the pensioner, carries the same disease, and it is passed on from generation to generation.
note: Calls Russians as a people slaves, animals and diseased.

text: The Russian government bears full responsibility for the invasion and for the crimes committed by its forces. Its officials have lied to their own citizens, jailed thousands of protesters and silenced independent media. Accountability must reach those who planned and ordered the war, not ordinary people who never had a real say in the decision.
note: Harsh criticism of the Russian government, explicitly not of Russians as a people.

text: Human rights groups in Germany reported a rise in harassment of Russian-speaking residents after February 2022, including insults in shops and vandalism at Russian grocery stores. Local officials condemned the incidents and stressed that people living in Germany should not be held responsible for the decisions of the Kremlin.
note: News about anti-Russian harassment that condemns it; the text is not hostile.

text: FACT CHECK: Did Ukraine run secret US-funded bioweapons labs? No. The claim, promoted by Russia's defence ministry in March 2022, refers to public-health laboratories that the United States helped upgrade under a programme to secure dangerous pathogens left over from the Soviet era. The World Health Organization and independent experts found no evidence of weapons research.
note: Fact-check attributing a claim to the Russian defence ministry and refuting it.

text: A viral post claims that Russia banned the sale of jeans in 2024 because they are 'a symbol of Western decadence'. This is false. We found no law, decree or regulation restricting the sale of denim, and jeans remain on sale in major Russian shops. The post originated on a satirical website and was later shared without its original context.
note: Debunks a viral claim about a Russian law.

text: In his annual address, the Russian president said Western sanctions had 'completely failed' and that the economy was growing faster than Europe's. Economists interviewed for this article said the claim left out key context: growth was driven mainly by military spending, while high inflation, labour shortages and a weaker rouble were squeezing ordinary households.
note: Critical analysis of an official's claim.

text: Russia's central bank raised its key interest rate to 21 percent in October 2024, the highest level in more than two decades, in an effort to slow inflation that was running at around 9 percent. Higher borrowing costs made mortgages and business loans considerably more expensive, and several large companies postponed investment projects as a result.
note: States economic facts in its own voice; no claim by others is reported.

text: Russia's Lake Baikal, in southern Siberia, is the deepest lake in the world, reaching 1,642 metres, and holds about a fifth of the planet's unfrozen fresh surface water. It is fed by more than 300 rivers and streams but drained by only one, the Angara. Its waters are home to the Baikal seal, one of the few freshwater seal species.
note: Encyclopedic description in its own voice.

text: The cruiser Moskva, flagship of Russia's Black Sea Fleet, sank in April 2022 after being struck by two Ukrainian Neptune anti-ship missiles off the coast near Odesa. It was the largest warship lost in combat since the Falklands War in 1982, and its loss pushed the remaining Russian ships further away from the Ukrainian coast.
note: War facts stated in its own voice; no reported claim.
